problem_shape: These papers share a practical pressure: important systems are making decisions that people cannot safely accept as silent guesses. The decision may be whether an image is illegal abuse material, why a social-media post signals humanitarian need, which graph edges can be removed, why a recommendation was made, whether a meme is harmful, why a machine looks anomalous, or which evidence in a hate video supports a label. In each case the output is not enough. A correct-looking answer still leaves the user unable to check whether the system used the right clues, ignored noise, followed domain rules, or broke under small changes. The family is therefore about turning hidden model behavior into inspectable evidence. Some papers expose parts, such as concepts, paths, roles, labels, subgraphs, event interactions, spatial cues, or retrieved facts. Others add interfaces, agents, or reports so a person can question the result. The shared real-world problem is accountability under complexity: when data comes from images, text, graphs, sequences, user histories, auctions, maintenance streams, or counseling dialogue, the system must show what mattered and why.
naive_failure: A smart beginner might try two simple fixes. The first is to use a more accurate model and trust the score. That fails because a high score does not say whether the model relied on a face, a body cue, a graph path, a cultural symbol, a noisy chat turn, or a misleading popular item. The second is to ask the model to explain itself afterward in plain language. That also fails when the explanation is only a story placed on top of the decision. Several papers explicitly worry about explanations that are brittle, disconnected, one-time, or not faithful to the actual behavior. Graph explainers can ignore sign patterns or produce broken subgraphs. Search and dialogue systems can explain noisy context instead of the useful signal. Multimodal classifiers can name the wrong text or image clue. In sensitive settings, a plausible explanation can be worse than none because it creates trust without giving a real way to check the decision.
mathematical_principle: The recurring mathematical idea is evidence assignment: break a decision into candidate pieces, then estimate which pieces changed the outcome and which pieces merely came along for the ride. The pieces differ by setting. In a graph, they can be edges, paths, node roles, communities, attributes, or relation types. In text and images, they can be words, regions, captions, visual concepts, cultural references, or label-linked fragments. In recommendations, they can be user actions, social subgraphs, popularity signals, causal mediators, or item features. In streams and maintenance, they can be event types, timestamps, interaction patterns, or anomaly causes. The math turns these pieces into things that can be compared, scored, hidden, kept, or removed. Some papers measure contribution by removing or perturbing a part and watching how the answer changes. Some use paths or rules so evidence must form a coherent chain. Some compress the decision into concepts or prototypes so similar cases can share names. Some estimate uncertainty or noise so explanations stay compact without becoming fragile. The central tradeoff is simple explanation versus faithful detail: a useful explanation must be small enough for people to inspect, but not so small that it drops the real cause of the decision.
why_math_matters: The math matters because these systems are built on structured signals, not loose collections of facts. A signed social graph has friendly and hostile links, so an explanation for a link prediction should respect how signs combine along paths. A heterogeneous graph has different kinds of nodes and relations, so noise removal must know which relations mean the same thing and which do not. A crisis post pairs text and image evidence, so a rationale transferred from words to pixels must preserve the reason for the label across modes. A meme can be harmful because of the clash between a picture, a joke, and cultural knowledge, not because one word is toxic. A counseling agent needs stage-consistent reasoning because emotional support changes from exploration to insight to action. These papers use scoring, path constraints, concept grouping, relation-aware denoising, information gain, uncertainty estimates, and rule-like reasoning because the world already has parts and connections. The math gives researchers a way to say what should count as a better explanation: more faithful to the decision, more stable under noise, more compact, more human-queryable, more tied to domain concepts, or more useful for intervention.
paper_family: The representative papers are siblings because they all replace opaque output with structured evidence. Age classification in child sexual abuse material does this by fusing expert-recognized cues such as face, body proportions, and sexual characteristics instead of leaving the decision inside one end-to-end model. Graph papers form a large branch: Shapley-based sparsification scores edge importance, SGExplainer requires balanced signed paths, GNN Explainers 2.0 asks for layer-wise provenance, robust heterogeneous graph explanations separate relation-aware signal from structural noise, and node role-guided clustering turns changing graph groups into named roles. Language-model papers attack the same hidden-behavior problem in recommendations, counseling, conversational search, SQL checking, auto-bidding, and hate-video analysis by making reasoning, retrieved evidence, labels, reports, or action layers explicit. Multimodal papers add another branch: humanitarian classification transfers rationales from text to images, meme and vaccine-misinformation work grounds labels in cultural or visual concepts, and geo-localization uses spatial semantics to make cross-view matching less mysterious. Recommendation and social papers explain synergistic effects, popularity bias, multi-behavior preference, federated contribution, and influential node groups. Across all branches, the deeper move is the same: expose the path from raw signal to decision.
what_changed: The 2026 version of this family is broader than classic feature importance. The evidence shows explanations moving into deployed, mixed-data settings: psychological support, emotional dialogue, predictive maintenance, auto-bidding, federated recommendation, graph foundation models, hate video analysis, medical diagnosis, and misinformation detection. Large language models appear often, but usually as one part of an explanation system rather than as trusted narrators. There is also more attention to robustness: explanations should survive graph perturbations, adversarial retrieval changes, noisy context, out-of-context media, missing modalities, and shifting user behavior. The family is moving from static explanations for a single prediction toward evidence that can be queried, transferred across data types, used for debugging, and tied to decisions people must act on.
limits: These outputs depend on assumptions that the input evidence cannot fully prove. An explanation is useful only if the exposed pieces really caused the decision, not merely matched a human-friendly story. Concept-based methods assume the chosen concepts cover the important cues. Graph explanations assume links, signs, roles, and relation types carry real meaning rather than noise or historical bias. Multimodal rationales assume text and image clues can be aligned without losing culture-specific meaning. Agent explanations assume the visible reasoning steps reflect the system's actual choice process. Compact explanations can hide secondary causes, while detailed explanations can overwhelm users. The evidence here reports problems, approaches, and selected contributions; it does not establish that these methods remain faithful across platforms, cultures, adversarial settings, medical contexts, legal review, or future data shifts.
